title: A Note towards the Understanding of Lighting Quality
authors: R. J. Hawkes, D. L. Loe & E. Rowlands, 1979
research_question: To gain some understanding of the nature of lighting quality by evaluating qualitative aspects of different lighting situations.

participants.description: 15 males and 13 females, age range 20 to 65 years (high proportion below 40 years), secretarial, technical and academic staff from the Bartlett School of Architecture and Planning, University College London.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A windowless office mock-up (10 ft x 15 ft x 8 ft high, 3m x 4.5m x 2.4m) furnished as a two-person office, equipped with six different types of dimmer-controlled luminaires (ceiling recessed, wall lighting, downlights, desk lights, light tracks with spotlights). 18 distinct lighting situations were created and presented.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Experimental design and procedure, Table 2.1, Figure 2.1, 2.2, 2.3

measures.instrument: Numerical rating scale (1-100 units, anchored by situations 1 & 2 as 100)
15 semantic differential scales (e.g., Frugal-Lavish, Focused-Diffuse, Dim-Bright, Simple-Complex, Mysterious-Obvious)
Photometer (measured at 4 ft height, facing subject's direction of sight)
Photometer (average illuminance over a small sphere)
Photometer (magnitude of difference in illuminances on opposite sides of a flat surface)
Calculated from illumination vector and mean spherical illuminance
Photometer (average luminance over curved surface of a small cylinder)
Eastman contrast threshold visibility meter (at desktop level)
Photocell with acceptance angle of ±50° about the normal to the photocell surface
Calculated (percentage of observers judging situation comfortable)
Sum of judgments on pleasant-unpleasant and attractive-unattractive semantic differential scales

findings.antecedent: Diffuse lighting sources (wall-lighting or recessed)
findings.quote: All eight situations using diffuse sources only... are placed towards the uninteresting side of the neutral on this factor

findings.antecedent: Focused lighting sources (one or more)
findings.quote: all 10 situations with one or more focused sources are towards the interesting side of neutral.

findings.antecedent: More boundaries separating areas of light and shade in a relatively sharp contour
findings.mechanism: The importance of boundaries in visual perception (Gestalt psychologists' Figure-Ground phenomenon).
findings.quote: the more 'interesting' situations have more boundaries separating areas of light and shade in a relatively sharp contour.

findings.antecedent: Variation in luminance distribution (e.g., wide range, multiple peaks)
findings.mechanism: Articulation, distinction between focal areas and general background, which distinguishes the special and mysterious, from the commonplace and obvious.
findings.quote: the subjective experience of interest might arise when the variation in luminance in a space has a particular type of distribution.

findings.antecedent: Lighting situations that are both brighter (high Factor I score) and more complex (high Factor II score)
findings.mechanism: Both brightness and complexity factors must operate together for higher preference.
findings.quote: the brighter more complex situations being the highest point on the contour map

findings.antecedent: Situations using only one type of luminaire
findings.quote: situations using only one type of luminaire occur lower down on the slopes

findings.antecedent: Common recessed luminaires
findings.quote: particularly the common recessed luminaires... occur lower down on the slopes

findings.antecedent: Smaller source luminaires with more directional quality
findings.quote: the smaller source luminaires, with more directional quality, are concentrated towards the preference peak.

findings.antecedent: Higher energy consumption (watts)
findings.mechanism: Inefficient concentrated tungsten sources were associated with higher preference, leading to higher energy consumption.
findings.quote: the peaks (lightest shading) being the highest energy consuming situation in terms of watts... iso-consumption contours are comparable with the iso-preference ones.

findings.antecedent: Regular arrays of recessed luminaires (most common way of lighting offices)
findings.mechanism: Possibly due to lack of visual variety in a windowless environment, low quality of prismatic 'batwing' luminaires, or experimental procedure not allowing long work time making variety more desirable.
findings.quote: the regular arrays of recessed luminaires, the most common way of lighting offices, are the least preferred.

findings.antecedent: Lighting design with complexity and brightness
findings.quote: Complexity and brightness together: perhaps that is what people want in the lighting of their offices.

mechanisms: The subjective experience of interest might arise when the variation in luminance in a space has a particular type of distribution, creating articulation and distinction between focal areas and general background.
More 'interesting' situations have more boundaries separating areas of light and shade in a relatively sharp contour.
Both brightness and complexity factors must operate together for higher preference.
Lack of visual variety in a windowless environment may exaggerate low ratings of lighting situations.
The quality of specific luminaires (e.g., prismatic 'batwing') can influence preference.
Experimental procedures that do not allow long exposure times may make variety more desirable.
moderators: Situation K (anomalous situation for brightness perception)
Windowless environment (exaggerating low ratings for recessed luminaires)
Experimental procedure duration (not allowing long work time)
implementation_implications: Designers should aim for lighting designs that incorporate both complexity and brightness to enhance preference in offices.
Alternatives to regular arrays of recessed luminaires should be considered for office lighting.
The quality of specific luminaire types should be improved, especially those rated poorly (e.g., prismatic 'batwing').

tables.description: Lists the 18 lighting situations and the luminaires used for each.
Shows the Latin-square design for the order of presentation of lighting situations to subjects.
Presents physical measures (various illuminance values in lux) and energy consumption in watts for all 18 lighting situations.
Shows factor loadings for 13 semantic differential scales on Factor I (Brightness) and Factor II (Interest).
Lists Factor I (Brightness) scores, Factor II (Interest) scores, and Preference Ratings for each of the 18 lighting situations.
Presents correlations of brightness factor scores with various illuminance measures for 18 situations and for 17 situations (excluding K).

limitations: The multidimensional scaling analysis (MDSCAL) did not produce an intuitively reasonable result, possibly due to the sequential presentation of random mock-ups rather than simultaneous comparison.
The experimental procedure did not allow subjects to work for a long time in the same environment, which might have made variety more desirable.
The study was conducted in a windowless environment, which might have exaggerated the low ratings of situations lacking visual variety.

The generalizability of the preference trend (increasing with brightness and complexity) to extreme values is unknown, making it unclear whether a maximizing or optimizing design procedure is required.
